v.q: In ACID, what does the "A" guarantee?
o: All steps of a transaction succeed together or none take effect
Data stays available on every node even during failures
Concurrent transactions can never see each other's changes
Each transaction is executed on the fastest replica only
v.w: Atomicity means all-or-nothing. A failure halfway rolls every step back. Availability is a different idea, from CAP.

v.q: Which statement about atomicity is NOT true?
o: It makes concurrent transactions invisible to each other
A failure halfway rolls every step back
It is often implemented with a write-ahead log
It means all steps happen or none do
v.w: Hiding concurrent work is isolation. Atomicity is all-or-nothing, usually through undo information in a log.

v.q: A transfer debits account A, then the server crashes before crediting B. Which ACID property makes the debit disappear after recovery?
o: Atomicity, using the write-ahead log to undo partial work
Isolation, because other transactions never see the debit
Consistency, because balances must always stay positive
Durability, because committed data survives the crash
v.w: The write-ahead log lets the database undo uncommitted changes on restart. That is atomicity in practice.

v.q: A transfer is half done when the server crashes. After restart the debit is gone and the credit never happened. Which property did the database honour?
o: Atomicity
Availability
Durability of the uncommitted debit
Eventual consistency
v.w: Uncommitted work is undone from the log, so the transaction leaves no trace. Durability applies only to committed data.

o: Once a commit is acknowledged, the data survives a crash
The database can never go down while handling writes
Stored data is always encrypted with a strong cipher
Old versions of every row are kept forever for audit
v.w: Durability is usually delivered by flushing the write-ahead log to disk before acknowledging the commit.

v.q: Which statement about durability is NOT true?
o: It guarantees the database never goes down
It usually relies on flushing the log to disk
It applies once the commit is acknowledged
It means committed data survives a crash
v.w: Durability is about surviving a crash, not about avoiding one. Availability is a separate property.

v.q: Which isolation problem occurs when a transaction reads a row twice and gets different values because another transaction committed in between?
o: Non-repeatable read: the same row returns a different value
Dirty read: the transaction sees uncommitted changes
Phantom read: new rows appear in a repeated range query
Lost update: two writers silently overwrite each other
v.w: A dirty read sees uncommitted data. A non-repeatable read sees two different committed values of the same row. A phantom read sees new or missing rows in a repeated range query.

v.q: Two reads of the same account row inside one transaction return 500 and then 400 after another transaction commits. Which isolation level removes this problem?
o: Repeatable read
Read uncommitted
Read committed
Autocommit
v.w: Repeatable read keeps the value a transaction has already read stable. Read committed still allows a non-repeatable read.

v.q: What does BASE stand for in the context of distributed data stores?
o: Basically Available, Soft state, Eventual consistency
Balanced, Atomic, Serializable, Efficient replication
Backup, Archive, Snapshot and Export for every node
Basic Atomic Storage Engine with strict consistency
v.w: BASE trades strict consistency for availability and scale: the system keeps answering and replicas converge over time.

v.q: Which statement about BASE is NOT true?
o: It guarantees strict consistency after every write
The system stays available during failures
State may change over time without new input
Replicas converge eventually
v.w: BASE trades immediate consistency for availability. Strong consistency after every write is the ACID side.

v.q: Which system is the better fit for an account ledger where a balance must never be wrong, even briefly?
o: A relational database with ACID transactions
An eventually consistent key-value store
A cache in front of the database with a long TTL
A full-text search index fed by change events
v.w: Money needs strong consistency and atomic multi-row updates. Eventual consistency suits feeds, counters and caches.

v.q: Which data is best kept in an eventually consistent store?
o: A product view counter
A customer account balance
A payment authorization record
An inventory reservation for the last item
v.w: A slightly stale counter harms nobody. Balances, authorizations and last-item stock need strong consistency.

v.q: A shopping-style social feed shows a like count that is a few seconds stale on some replicas. Which description fits?
o: Eventual consistency, an accepted BASE trade-off
A violation of atomicity inside one transaction
A durability failure after a database crash
A deadlock between two competing transactions
v.w: Replicas that lag but converge are eventually consistent. For a like count that trade-off buys availability and speed.

v.q: Which system behaviour is a sign of BASE, not ACID?
o: Two replicas briefly return different values
A failed transfer leaves both balances unchanged
A commit is acknowledged only after the log is flushed
A transaction cannot see uncommitted rows
v.w: Brief divergence between replicas that later converge is eventual consistency. The other three are ACID guarantees.

v.q: Which statement about ACID versus BASE is correct?
o: They are ends of a spectrum, and systems often pick per operation
BASE databases are unable to commit data at all
ACID databases can never be run across several nodes
BASE guarantees stronger consistency than ACID does
v.w: Real systems mix them: for example strong consistency for payments and eventual consistency for analytics in the same product.

v.q: Which statement about choosing ACID or BASE is NOT true?
o: A system must pick one model for all its data
Payments often need strong consistency
Analytics can accept eventual consistency
The choice can be made per operation
v.w: Real products mix both, so the choice is made per operation or per data set.
